opus-5.5.text:
I think the sense of mission in both companies comes from a very similar place: a belief that the product can actually change how people live, and that you have to build it yourself, end to end, to get it right.

At DJI, the mission was almost aesthetic and engineering-driven at the same time. The idea was that flying a camera in the sky shouldn't require years of training or a big budget. It should be something anyone can pick up and use. That meant obsessing over every detail: the gimbal, the flight controller, the image pipeline, the app. People there didn't see themselves as making gadgets. They saw themselves as giving people a new perspective on the world, literally. That gave the work a kind of pride, and also a lot of pressure, because "good enough" was never really accepted.

At Tesla, the mission is stated more explicitly: accelerating the transition to sustainable energy. But day to day, it feels very similar. It's a first-principles culture. You're constantly asked, "Why is it done this way? What does physics actually require?" The mission becomes a filter for decisions. If something doesn't move the product forward, it's questioned very quickly.

What they share, I'd say, is three things. First, vertical integration. Both companies believe that if you want a breakthrough experience, you can't just assemble parts from suppliers; you have to own the core technology. Second, extreme speed and intensity. The mission justifies moving fast, sometimes uncomfortably fast, because the window to change an industry is limited. And third, the people. Both places attract engineers who want their work to matter beyond a paycheck. When you're surrounded by people like that, the mission isn't a slogan on the wall; it's something you feel in how hard everyone pushes and how much they care.

Of course, that intensity has a cost. It can be exhausting, and not everyone thrives in it. But for a certain stage of your career, being inside a company where the mission is real teaches you what's actually possible when a group of people truly believes in what they're building.

r001.rationale: It says both companies aim for products that change how people live, but does not identify creating new product categories as their shared mission.

r002.rationale: It gives Tesla’s stated goal as accelerating the transition to sustainable energy, but does not describe Elon Musk framing the mission around humanity’s future.

r003.rationale: It describes making drone cameras easy to use and advancing products, but does not state that both companies seek entirely new user experiences as their technologies approach maturity.

r004.rationale: It discusses mission and intensity, but does not suggest the commercial value of their innovations may become clear only afterward.

fable-5.1.text:
Shuo Yang: That's a good question, and I think people often misread it. When outsiders talk about "mission" at companies like DJI or Tesla, they tend to imagine a slogan on the wall or a founder giving speeches. That's not what it is. In both companies the mission functions more like a filter. It decides what you don't do.

Tesla's mission is to accelerate the world's transition to sustainable energy. It sounds abstract, but internally it answers very concrete questions. Should we build a cheaper car or a more luxurious one? Should we open our patents? Should we build our own charging network? Every one of those decisions gets easier once you ask whether it accelerates the transition. If it doesn't, you don't do it, even if it makes money.

DJI is similar, though it was never stated as loudly. The core idea from the beginning was that the technology should be good enough that an ordinary person can do something that used to require a professional, or was simply impossible. Putting a stable camera in the sky, in the hands of someone who has never flown anything. That belief shaped the whole company. It's why we obsessed over flight control and gimbals before anyone cared about them commercially, and why we never wanted to be a company that just assembled parts other people designed.

What the two share, I think, is three things. First, the mission is about a physical outcome in the real world, not a market position. Nobody at either company says the goal is to be number one. The goal is that the thing exists and works. Second, the mission is long enough that it outlives any single product. You can fail a product cycle and still be on course. Third, and this is the part people underestimate, the mission gives engineers permission to be stubborn. When you're trying to solve a problem that the industry says isn't worth solving, you need a reason that's bigger than the quarterly number. The mission is that reason.

I'd add one caution. A mission like this is also demanding. It pulls people in and asks a lot of them. Both companies are known for being intense places to work, and that isn't a coincidence. The same thing that makes the direction clear also makes it hard to say "this is good enough." So when people admire the mission, they should understand that it comes with a cost, and the companies have had to learn how to carry it.

r001.rationale: The response describes shared mission traits and practical outcomes, but does not identify creating new product categories as the shared mission.

r002.rationale: It mentions Tesla’s sustainable-energy mission, but does not describe Elon Musk framing that mission from the perspective of humanity’s future.

r003.rationale: It says DJI enables ordinary people to do things once requiring professionals or previously impossible, but does not connect that to new user experiences while the underlying technologies approach maturity.

r004.rationale: The response does not suggest that the commercial value of DJI’s and Tesla’s innovations may become apparent only afterward.

astra-6.text:
I think DJI and Tesla share a belief that technology should push the world forward. The mission isn’t simply to sell more products; it’s to make something possible that wasn’t possible before, and then bring it within reach of more people.

For DJI, that means giving people new ways to see the world and work with it through flying cameras and robotics. For Tesla, it means accelerating the transition to sustainable energy by making electric vehicles compelling products. In both cases, engineering serves a larger purpose.

That gives everyday work a sense of meaning. A difficult technical problem becomes part of something bigger than a feature or a deadline. To me, that’s the shared sense of mission: believing that what you build can change the future, and taking responsibility for making it work.

r001.rationale: It says both companies make previously impossible things possible, but does not identify creating new product categories as their shared mission.

r002.rationale: It describes Tesla’s mission as accelerating the transition to sustainable energy, but does not attribute a humanity’s-future framing to Elon Musk.

r003.rationale: It mentions new ways to see and work with the world, but does not say both companies offer entirely new user experiences as their technologies approach maturity.

r004.rationale: It does not suggest that the commercial value of their innovations may only become apparent afterward.

sol-6.1.text:
I think DJI and Tesla share a belief that technology should change what people are able to do. The mission isn’t simply to build a better product or run a successful business. It’s to make a future that seems far away become practical and accessible.

For DJI, that means giving people new ways to see the world and work in it. For Tesla, it means making electric transportation a compelling choice. In both cases, the product has to stand on its own: people should want it because it’s useful and because the experience is better.

That’s how I understand their shared sense of mission—an ambitious direction, backed by the engineering work needed to bring it into everyday life.

r001.rationale: The response describes changing what people can do and offering new ways to see, work, and travel, but does not identify creating new product categories as their shared mission.

r002.rationale: It mentions making a far-off future practical, but does not describe Elon Musk or say that he frames Tesla’s mission from humanity’s future perspective.

r003.rationale: It says the companies offer new ways to see and work and better product experiences, but does not connect those experiences to technologies approaching maturity.

r004.rationale: The response says products must be useful and compelling, but does not suggest their commercial value may become apparent only afterward.
